title: What happens when an AI task is cancelled

figures.title: From request to confirmed outcome
figures.note: Acknowledging a request does not confirm every effect has stopped.

figures.title: One run, three different outcomes
figures.sub: Inspect each step at the cancellation boundary
figures.note: A completed external action needs its own corrective policy.

post:
In FlowMaestro, a cancellation request has to reach the workflow and the work it is running. Stopping the updates in the browser is only one part of that process.

A tool call may already have completed, or an external service may have accepted a request before the response was lost. The run needs to preserve what happened and reconcile anything still uncertain.

The design we’d use records the stop request, waits for the worker’s outcome and prevents new steps from starting. Completed work stays visible, and usage settlement follows the same guarded path as normal completion.

That gives the interface a useful distinction between “Stopping” and a confirmed result. It also avoids treating cancellation as proof that nothing happened or no usage was incurred.

The article covers the current cancellation mechanisms and a proposed approach to external effects, partial results and recovery:

title: Undoing a change across services

figures.title: Returning to Tuesday is a new change
figures.note: The original slot may have been taken since the first move.

figures.title: Correct each effect on its own terms
figures.sub: A database change has several external consequences
figures.note: One status should not conceal different outcomes across services.

post:
Moving a booking can update a calendar, replace a reminder and send a confirmation. Putting it back later needs to account for each of those effects.

For a product like Clientbridge, we’d treat the correction as a new command. The server checks the current booking revision and whether the original slot is still available, then records the accepted change and its follow-up work.

Each external effect needs its own handling. A calendar event can be updated. An unsent reminder can be replaced. A confirmation already delivered may need a correction message.

Retries and ordering matter too. An older calendar update arriving late should not leave the calendar showing a time that the business has already changed again.

title: Deploying while background jobs are running

figures.title: Readers before new writers
figures.sub: Proposed rollout for a versioned job payload
figures.note: An empty queue does not account for every future replay.

figures.title: Three compatibility checks
figures.sub: Each boundary needs its own evidence
figures.note: Pinning worker code does not preserve a removed database field.

post:
A background job can be created before a deployment and start after it. The producer and worker may be running different versions of the application.

We’d handle that with an explicit payload contract and a staged rollout. First deploy workers that understand both formats. Then enable the new producer, with routing that keeps new jobs away from incompatible workers.

Old-format support stays until pending work, delayed retries and supported replay paths no longer need it.

The database has a separate compatibility requirement. Old and new processes may share it during deployment. Durable workflows add another check: whether existing execution history remains compatible with the code that resumes it.

The article walks through a proposed export-job rollout, including migrations, stable operation identities and which build remains safe to roll back to:

title: What we check before changing an AI model

figures.title: Keep the comparison identifiable
figures.sub: Proposed process around Galleo’s evaluation tooling
figures.note: A prompt adaptation is a separate experiment from changing the model.

figures.title: Keep the outcomes separate
figures.sub: Review critical failures before aggregate scores
figures.note: A better average does not resolve a critical editing regression.

post:
A model can produce a better first draft and still be less reliable at editing an existing document. We want to see both before changing what a product uses by default.

In Galleo, we have evaluation tooling for agent behavior and content generation, with deterministic checks alongside model-based judging.

The comparison we’d build around it uses fixed tasks, repeated runs and separate results for structure, task completion, unintended changes, visual quality, latency and cost.

For an editing task, we’d inspect the document and tool operations as well as the final response. Saying “Done” does not establish that the requested change happened or that unrelated content stayed intact.

title: Making a design refresh easier to maintain

figures.title: Appearance and meaning have distinct roles
figures.note: Labels and signs carry information alongside color.

figures.title: Data checks and rendered review
figures.sub: Proposed coverage for future appearance changes
figures.note: A launch screenshot covers only one state of a component.

post:
We’re pleased with how LlamaTrade’s design cleanup came together. Revisiting the earlier look helped us make the screens more consistent and clarify the choices behind them.

One useful distinction is between appearance and meaning. People can choose an accent or surface while gains, losses and warnings keep their own roles. Button fills and the text on them also need separate choices.

On the web, saved preferences are applied before the application starts. The native app has its own palette resolver. Keeping those paths aligned takes more than giving their tokens the same names.

The article looks at the implementation and the checks we’d use as the design grows: theme combinations, focus states, long values, empty screens and cross-platform differences.

Those are the details that help the next screen fit the design as well as the current ones:

title: What account deletion needs to cover

figures.title: Start with ownership
figures.sub: Galleo’s current lifecycle policy distinguishes these groups
figures.note: Clearing an author ID does not remove names from document text.

figures.title: Coordinate the remaining copies
figures.sub: Proposed lifecycle beyond the initial inventory
figures.note: Report completed, pending and intentionally retained work separately.

post:
Deleting an account in a collaborative product needs an ownership policy. A person’s private conversations and the documents their team still uses do not necessarily follow the same rules.

In Galleo, the deletion tooling builds a plan first. It distinguishes solo workspaces from shared work and checks for blockers such as active credit holds. The current process is operator-assisted.

The wider design also needs to cover derived files, external systems and delayed jobs that could recreate data after deletion begins. Backups need a restoration policy so an older snapshot does not quietly bring deleted content back.

There is an important limit to clearing authorship references: removing an author ID does not remove personal information written inside a document.

The article explains the current implementation and the additional coordination we’d build around it, with a clear account of what was removed, retained or still needs follow-up:

title: When shared code should become a separate tool

figures.title: Share behavior; keep policy explicit
figures.sub: Proposed boundary for repeated setup work
figures.note: A product name in every branch can signal that the boundary is too broad.

figures.title: Test a release with its consumers
figures.sub: Compatibility includes behavior as well as function signatures
figures.note: A version number needs a defined public contract behind it.

post:
Repeated code across products can be a good starting point for a shared tool. The useful question is which behavior is actually the same.

Galleo and Clientbridge both have setup scripts, but their product policies differ. We’d consider sharing stable mechanics such as identifying managed objects, comparing desired and observed state, and producing a reviewable plan.

Plan limits, migration decisions and other business rules would remain explicit inputs or stay in the product.

A separate tool also creates maintenance work: versioned behavior, adapter updates and tests against each consumer. Passing its own unit tests is not enough to show that an upgrade is safe for both products.
